newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb Karadzic still power behind the scenes.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb Karadzic still power behind the scenes.

text.p: Former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, who revelled in his defiance of the world in wartime before being officially driven from power, is still making his presence felt in peacetime.

Karadzic, an indicted war criminal, no longer holds office but continues to wield power in Bosnia's Serb republic, working to ensure that his ultra-nationalist policies remain in place, diplomats say.

"He still pulls the strings, he still holds meetings with the leadership of the Serb republic," Michael Steiner, the deputy High Representative to Bosnia, told Reuters. "He has ministers reporting to him directly."

The former psychiatrist and his associates, who orchestrated an "ethnic cleansing" campaign during the Bosnian war, are obstructing the Dayton peace agreement at almost every level, Steiner and other diplomats say.

The Serb leadership has refused to allow Moslem or Croat refugees to return to their homes, blocked the formation of a single central bank, failed to meet arms control limits and signed a cooperation pact with neighbouring Yugoslavia in clear violation of the peace treaty.
Charged with crimes against humanity, Karadzic has dismissed the U.N. war crimes tribunal as a "political court" and lives in Serb territory guarded by heavily-armed police.
Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic are among dozens of war crimes suspects who have refused to face trial before the tribunal in the Hague.
Mladic keeps a low profile and has stayed out of the public arena since the peace treaty was signed in 1995.
But Karadzic has tightened his grip on power since fighting ended in 1995, asserting control over the army which had accused his party of rampant corruption.

Diplomats say Karadzic was a key player behind the cooperation pact agreed between Bosnian Serbs and Yugoslavia in February. The accord, brokered without consulting the Serbs' Moslem and Croat partners in the postwar government, was condemned as a serious breach of the Dayton peace treaty.
After international pressure forced Karadzic to step down from office last year, U.S. and European governments had hoped he would gradually be marginalised the longer he stayed out of the spotlight.

Instead, his defiant hand still guides decisions which are frustrating an expensive reconstruction effort, said Hrair Balian of the London-based International Crisis Group, a private agency which monitors the Bosnian peace process.
"There is a growing realisation in the international community that Karadzic is still a problem," said Balian, director of ICG's Sarajevo office.
The NATO-led peace force, fearing casualties or a possible backlash, has made clear that it does not want to launch any "manhunt" for indicted war criminals.
But diplomats say Karadzic and the "war crimes issue" will not go away, no matter how much money and effort is devoted to building the peace in Bosnia,

Without the prosecution of war crimes suspects, they say efforts to return refugees to their homes or to build reconciliation among the country's Moslem, Croat and Serb communities could be doomed to failure.
While major powers mull over how to reduce Karadzic's influence, NATO soldiers and Western diplomats in Bosnia have to take care to avoid an awkward encounter with the fugitive.
American diplomat Robert Beecroft said in a speech recently that when he travelled to the government seat of Pale for a meeting, he saw what appeared to be Karadzic's black limousine.
"I had to ascertain that he wasn't in the building before I could enter it," Beecroft said.
